cashflow_rationale:
Free cash flow, as the company defines it, has been negative every year: -£299M in FY2022, -£360M in FY2023, -£392M in FY2024, -£410M in FY2025 and -£198M in H1 2026. Only individual Q4s were positive (+£5M in Q4 2025, +£2M in Q4 2024), helped by year-end collections.

The structure is the problem, not the cycle. Capex, including technology access fees, was £397M in FY2023, £401M in FY2024 and £341M in FY2025, and is guided at about £300M for FY2026 within a £1.7bn programme for FY2026 to FY2030. Net cash interest was £143M in FY2025, is guided at about £160M for FY2026, and runs higher once a full year of the SONIA+675bps term loan is included. Together that is about £480-510M a year against LTM adjusted EBITDA of £174M and a record high of £306M in FY2023.

Q2 2026 FCF before interest was close to breakeven (-£81M including £73M of interest), and management expects FY2026 FCF close to the H1 outflow. The business is capital-heavy (PP&E and £1.6bn of intangibles, mostly capitalised development). Specials deposits give some working capital funding, but they unwind as cars are delivered.
circulo_rationale:
Outside the circle, for now. The industry mechanics are understood. Wholesale volume times ASP drives revenue, Specials drive the mix, and gross margin swings with dealer support, warranty and FX. Revenue is booked on wholesale to dealers, not on retail sales, so stock in the channel can flatter or depress a quarter. H1 2026 retail ran more than 30% ahead of wholesale while aged stock was cleared.

Three parts cannot yet be underwritten. First, the accounts rest on adjustments. D&A of £297M in FY2025 (guided at £375-400M for FY2026) is mostly amortisation of capitalised development, so adjusted EBITDA (£108M in FY2025) overstates cash earnings when capex is £300-340M a year. Second, Specials economics are opaque. My implied wholesale ASP for H1 2026 Specials is about £0.8M, while management quotes about £1.15M for Valhalla, presumably at retail (unverified). Third, the capital structure is now a legal question. The July 2026 financing moved almost 200 trademarks into a new unrestricted subsidiary, and bondholders are preparing a claim under New York law and section 423 of the UK Insolvency Act. How that ends is outside the analysis.
debt_rationale:
Net debt was £1,544.7M at 30 June 2026. That is gross debt of £1,661.1M: £1,345.2M of loan notes, £168.8M of bank loans (the RCF), £18.3M drawn on the Yew Tree facility, £89.7M of leases and £39.1M of inventory financing, less £114.9M of cash and £1.5M not available. The company's adjusted leverage is 8.9x LTM adjusted EBITDA of £174M (12.8x at FY2025). The 8.15x adjusted figure excludes leases and inventory financing (£1,415.9M / £173.8M). Net debt rose from £766M (FY2022) to £814M (FY2023), £1,163M (FY2024) and £1,380M (FY2025); the 3-year average for FY2023-FY2025 is £1,119M.

Maturities and cost. $1,050M of 10.0% notes and £565M of 10.375% notes, both senior secured, mature in March 2029. In July 2026 AML added a £450M senior secured term loan and a £100M delayed-draw loan from HPS at SONIA+675bps, maturing July 2031. The proceeds repaid the £170M RCF and the Yew Tree facility and took pro forma liquidity to about £340M, so pro forma net debt is roughly unchanged but gross debt is about £260M higher. Press reports put the USD notes at about 57 cents (yield to maturity about 37%) after the deal. The USD notes also move reported net debt with the exchange rate: a £72M revaluation gain in H1 2025, an £11M loss in H1 2026.

No convertibles. About 20M warrants remain exercisable until 2027. The ratio stored here is net debt / LTM adjusted EBITDA; FiscalAI's own figure (7.1x) uses a different EBITDA and debt definition.

The operating team is credible. The capital allocation record is not.

GOVERNANCE. Lawrence Stroll is Executive Chairman, and his Yew Tree Consortium holds 32.99% (FY2025 annual report: Yew Tree Overseas 16.18% and Ernesto Bertarelli 14.92% vote with him). The other shareholders with board nomination rights under separate relationship agreements are Geely/Li Shufu (14.08%), PIF (13.88%) and Mercedes-Benz (7.54%), so 68.5% of the shares sit with four blocs and the free float is about 31%. Adrian Hallmark (formerly CEO of Bentley) has been CEO since late 2024 and Doug Lafferty is CFO.

CAPITAL ALLOCATION. Equity came in repeatedly: FiscalAI shows share issuance of £847M in FY2020, £654M in FY2022, £326M in FY2023, £111M in FY2024 and £53M in FY2025. The share count went from about 824M in November 2023 to 1,010M in June 2026. Guidance was cut several times in 2024-2025, including a positive FY2025 adjusted EBIT target that ended at -£189M.

RELATED PARTIES. The Aston Martin F1 naming rights were sold to AMR GP, which Stroll controls, for £50M in Q1 2026. The group's AMR GP stake was sold in 2025. A £50M Yew Tree facility was arranged in April 2026 and repaid in July. Each deal eased liquidity, and each was a transaction with the controlling shareholder. The July 2026 financing with HPS put brand assets beyond the bondholders' collateral and drew a letter before action. Management's defence is that it bought liquidity (pro forma £340M), but it also created a creditor fight.
moat_rationale:
The brand is real and it sells scarcity. About 380 Valhallas were delivered between Q4 2025 and H1 2026 at a stated ASP of about £1.15M, the Valkyrie delivered 80 units in FY2022 and 87 in FY2023, and options contribute about 17-18% of core revenue. That is Intangible Assets.

It is not Pricing Power. Core ASP fell 5% in H1 2026 to £182k on dealer support to clear aged stock. Gross margin went from 39.1% in FY2023 to 29.4% in FY2025. With 5-6k units a year against Ferrari's roughly 14k and Porsche's roughly 300k (peer volumes unverified), AML carries a full OEM cost base (platforms, powertrain, compliance, tariffs) on a small base. Reported operating profit was negative in every year from FY2019 to FY2025 (FiscalAI). Ferrari runs at a 39% EBITDA margin, AML at 12% LTM.

The moat also shrank in 2026. Selling 50.1% of the non-automotive brand rights (lifestyle, licensing) to Authentic Brands, as a condition of the £100M delayed-draw tranche, hands a slice of the most durable asset to a third party.

management_rationale:
Suso Zamora (Chairman, President, and CEO) is well-known in the Peruvian sector and is also the CEO and Chairman of Enfoca, a Peruvian private equity fund with a strong track record of acquisitions. Luis Felipe Pinillos is the founder (an insider with skin in the game), former CEO (2009–2015 and 2019–2022), and Vice Chairman. He stepped down as CEO after the shareholder, Enfoca, joined the board, but he retains Class-B shares that carry 10:1 voting rights. Most of the current board members are partners at Enfoca. Oberrender, one of the directors, is a former CIO/Treasurer of UnitedHealth; he contributes valuable sector experience and independence, as he is not affiliated with Enfoca. The CFO is Gisele Remy, formerly of Alicorp and Belcorp.

An important aspect of Auna is its unique governance structure:

Dual-class share structure: It is a controlled company with dual-class shares.

Board independence: Because it is domiciled in Luxembourg and qualifies as a "controlled company" under NYSE rules, it adheres to Luxembourg practices. This means they are not required to have a majority of independent directors on the board.

Entrenched control: Enfoca holds 72.9% of the Class B shares, giving them ironclad control. Only three board directors are completely independent of Enfoca. Furthermore, the Audit and Risk Committee has only one truly independent director (the other two are considered independent under SEC rules, but as former Enfoca executives, their actual independence is limited).

Another detail that negatively impacts Auna involves the shares pledged through Heredia. Specifically, around 32 million of Enfoca's Class B shares are pledged in favor of lenders. A breach of the estimated (unofficial) ~$4 LTV (Loan-to-Value) threshold could lead lenders to foreclose on the pledged shares, potentially forcing a sale.
moat_rationale:
1. High switching costs: Oncosalud offers plans that compile all your information if you need cancer treatment: oncologists, medical history, treatments, etc. Switching to another plan involves a high cost. So, membership continues to grow and the claims loss ratio (MLR) is decreasing. Health plans are following the same trend, but the switching cost is lower, given that cancer treatment is more complex and delicate.
2. Intangible assets: licenses, accreditations, and government contracts (such as Trecca until 2046 to serve approximately 3 million beneficiaries or B2G ISSSTELEON in Mexico). 
3. Efficient scale: Complemeting the 2nd point, tangible assets such as beds and infrastructure make up this network and represent high barriers to entry (high CapEx to build many hospitals, "utility" type)

FCF (operating cash flow less PP&E and intangibles capex, FiscalAI) was positive every year from FY2021 to FY2025: €7.6M, €33.2M, €6.2M, €25.1M and €123.9M. Those advances are being passed on to suppliers: 1H26 operating cash flow was -€9.6M and FCF -€43.1M.

The next three years are negative by design. The plan carries €550–650M of capex over five years, of which €450–550M is for the US plant (hypothesis: figures from press coverage of the September 2025 plan, not from a filing), against EBITDA guided at €27–35M for FY2026. Positive is marked true on the FY2021–FY2025 record only.
circulo_rationale: The European business is readable: backlog turns into revenue by percentage of completion, customer advances fund working capital, and earnings follow launch cadence and booster output. What is not readable is the piece that justifies the price. The Virginia plant has no operating history, and Avio has not disclosed its unit economics: revenue per ton of propellant, the margin at 700 tons a year, or how much of the capacity is contracted. The MoUs with Raytheon and Lockheed Martin are non-binding. Two further layers are hard to model from outside: ESA contracting under the geographic-return rule, which sets how work and prices are allocated among member states, and the pass-through between IFRS revenues (€583.7M in FY2025) and the net revenues the company reports (€541.7M). The thesis rests on a plant that does not exist yet.

No financial debt. Total debt is €9.8M, all leases, against equity of €712.0M at 1H26 (debt/capital 1.4%). The net financial position was €535.7M of net cash at 1H26, -15.7x LTM EBITDA of €34.2M; pro forma for Advent's €109.4M in September 2026 it is about €645M, -18.9x.

Two caveats keep the green from meaning "excess cash". First, €690.3M of contract liabilities (customer advances) sit on the balance sheet, more than the cash itself; the cash is partly customer money that has to be spent delivering the backlog. Second, €450–550M is earmarked for the US plant. The base case leaves ~€350M of net cash at end-FY2029. Debt risk is low; the risk is capex overrun, not leverage. Debt/EBITDA field: -15.66x (net debt of -€535.7M over LTM EBITDA of €34.2M); gross debt/EBITDA is 0.29x.
management_rationale:
Giulio Ranzo has been CEO since October 2015 and was reappointed after the board renewal of 28 April 2026; Roberto Italia was reappointed Chairman at the same meeting, so the roles are separate. Director Elena Pisonero resigned in July 2026 and the board is co-opting a replacement. Insider shareholdings are not available in FiscalAI and were not verified.

Operating record: revenues grew (net revenues €357M in FY2022 to €541.7M in FY2025) and the backlog doubled (€1,014M to €2,166M), but margins did not hold. FY2019 EBITDA was €42.6M on a 10.9% margin; FY2025 was €32.3M on 5.5% (FiscalAI, IFRS revenue basis). The VV22 Vega C failure in December 2022 grounded the launcher for two years.

Capital allocation is now the whole story. The €400M rights issue of November 2025 was priced at €20.37, a deep discount, and took the share count from ~26.2M to ~46.8M. Advent then paid €33.40 for 3,275,268 new shares (€109.4M, 6.54%, 12-month lock-up) in September 2026, after Golden Power clearance. Both raises fund the US plant. Dividends continued (€6.8M paid in 2026, 58.6% payout per the FY2025 deck).

Ownership: Leonardo is the largest shareholder at ~18% after Advent, down from 19.3%; in October 2025 it sold 2,649,031 shares at ~€37.75 and then took up its rights. Delfin holds ~3.2%. The Italian state reviews control changes under Golden Power, which caps any takeover premium.
moat_rationale:
The barriers are real. Europe has room for one large solid-motor supplier, and Avio is it: Europropulsion (with ArianeGroup) is the only producer of the P120C/P160C boosters, and Avio has been prime on Vega since the programme started. Qualifying a solid motor on a missile such as Aster 30 or the Standard Missile's Mk 104 takes years, so a customer that has qualified Avio does not change supplier lightly. That is also why US primes are talking to a new entrant: the incumbent supply base (Northrop Grumman and L3Harris/Aerojet Rocketdyne) cannot meet demand.

The barriers do not show up in returns. EBITDA margin on IFRS revenues fell from 10.0% in FY2020 to 5.5% in FY2025, gross margin is 6.6%, and ROIC was 2.1% in FY2025 (FiscalAI). The main customers are ESA and national agencies, which contract close to cost. Institutional customers and geographic return protect the volume, not the price.

Operating cash flow (FiscalAI, consolidated, deployments and case proceeds run through operations): FY2021 -$585M, FY2022 -$466M, FY2023 -$275M, FY2024 +$217M, FY2025 -$29M, 1Q26 -$137M, 2Q26 +$52M. Positive in one of the last five fiscal years.

On Burford's own cash measures: cash receipts were $531M in FY2025 (258/48/118/107 by quarter) and $247M in 1H26, against deployments of $460M in FY2025 and $195M in 1H26. Adding ~$98M of cash opex and ~$78M of interest (inferred from the 1H26 cash bridge; hypothesis), the business consumed roughly $160M of cash in the half, covered by the January 2026 bond. Stable is false: quarterly receipts ranged from $48M to $310M over the last nine quarters. Asset-light is false: there is no capex, but the business is balance-sheet intensive, since every dollar of growth is a dollar deployed into cases for 2.5-3.5 years.
circulo_rationale:
The business model is simple to state and hard to underwrite from outside. Burford funds legal claims and gets paid a multiple of cost when they settle or win; 77% of concluded deployments settled, 14% won at adjudication and 9% lost (2Q26 deck). What an outside investor cannot see is the case-level evidence behind the marks: assets are carried at fair value under Burford's own model, and the YPF mark shows how far that can move. Burford-only YPF fair value was $1,689M at FY2025 year end and ~$101M at 2Q26 after one appellate ruling, a $1,596M write-down in 1Q26 on a position that had cost ~$126M.

The non-YPF book is diversified (hundreds of matters, top five assets 17% of modeled realizations), but durations are lengthening: weighted average life of active deployed cost is 3.5 years against 2.7 years for concluded assets, and the pre-pandemic vintages went from 3.4 to 5.3 years of WAL in 3.5 years. Red because the thesis rests on marks and on case outcomes we cannot verify independently.
debt_rationale:
Debt payable $2,403M, cash and marketable securities $733M, net debt $1,670M at 2Q26 (deck p.34). Total debt / total capital 74.6% ($2,403M / ($2,403M + $819M)); the Debt/EBITDA field holds 7.5x net debt over 2Q26 annualized EBIT, since LTM EBITDA is negative. Debt/TBV 3.5x and net debt/TBV 2.4x, from 0.9x and 0.7x at FY2025 year end. Management quoted leverage of 3.5x against a 2.0x debt-to-equity incurrence test on the 1Q26 call (3.5x matches debt/TBV; debt over total equity is 2.9x), so Burford can refinance but cannot add net new debt. There are no maintenance covenants. Moody's kept Ba1; S&P cut one notch to BB- (stable), per management on the 1Q26 call.

Net debt/EBITDA is not meaningful on LTM (EBIT is negative after the YPF write-down). 7.5x uses 2Q26 operating income before finance costs annualized ($55.9M x 4 = $224M); the adjusted 8.1x strips the $4.3M YPF mark from that quarter.

Maturities at 2Q26: $400M 2028 (6.25%), $360M 2030, $675M 2031, $500M 2033, $500M 2034 (8.50%); WAL 5.2 years, weighted cost 7.9%. In September 2026 Burford issued $300M of 8.00% senior secured notes due 2029 and will use them plus $100M of cash to retire the 2028 notes. That cuts gross debt by $100M but puts secured paper ahead of ~$2.0B of unsecured notes. No convertibles.
management_rationale:
Christopher Bogart (CEO, director) and Jonathan Molot (CIO) co-founded Burford in 2009 and have run it for 17 years. Capital allocation on YPF itself was good in cash terms: Burford sold part of its Petersen entitlement in the secondary market and management says it made more than $100M of cash profit on a position of ~$100M invested. But the same team let one case reach 40%+ of assets and funded growth with debt, which is why the reversal took equity from $2,448M to $819M.

After the ruling management cut ~$10M of annual compensation, suspended the interim dividend, ruled out buybacks, lost the CIO International (Craig Arnott) and named Travis Lenkner COO. The LTIP accrual reversal of $123M in 1H26 shows pay was tied to YPF marks, which cuts both ways.

GOVERNANCE. CEO and chair roles are separate; the board lists John Sievwright among non-executive directors (chair per company materials, not verified here). Insider ownership per FiscalAI: Molot 9.6M shares (4.4%), Bogart 1.37M (0.6%; FiscalAI may not capture all of his vehicles). Elizabeth O'Connell, formerly CFO and Bogart's spouse, remains an officer. No open-market insider purchases are recorded in FiscalAI since the March collapse, only award vestings, tax withholdings and a Molot trust reshuffle at $4.385 in August 2026.
moat_rationale:
Burford is the largest commercial legal-finance balance sheet: a $5.7B group-wide portfolio at 2Q26 and $3.9B of cumulative realizations since 2009. That record, the law-firm portfolio relationships (82% of pre-pandemic active cost sits in portfolio structures where new cases keep being added) and the ability to write $50M+ tickets are real advantages in origination; few rivals can fund a large antitrust or arbitration claim alone. New definitive commitments were $874M in FY2025 (sum of reported quarters) and $282M in 1H26.

The moat does not protect returns. Recent realizations show implied ROIC of 26-78% per quarter over the last eight quarters, below the 82% since inception, and the six largest concluded deals returned only 25-72% ROIC. Capital is the product, and Burford's cost of it rose after YPF: its newest paper is an 8.00% senior secured note (September 2026) against a 7.9% weighted average cost of debt. Yellow: franchise and origination edge yes, pricing power no.

cashflow_rationale:
HCC is experiencing high CapEx periods due to Blue Creek, and Cash From Ops is not compensating for this, so FCF has been negative since 2024 (FY2024 −$121M, troughing at −$274M on an LTM basis in Q2 2025). The drag is now narrowing quickly, however, LTM FCF has improved from −$274M to -$46M by Q2 2026, and the quarter itself was already FCF-positive (+$103M). Blue Creek is shifting from construction into production, and CapEx is rolling off its peak (LTM ~$347M vs. prior peaks of $460–530M), so the story is one of inflection rather than deterioration.

AMR, on the other side, was the best in this segment in the past, but since the coal price depreciation, net income is hitting Cash Flow From Ops hard, and with capex holding steady while operating cash flow collapsed, they have been FCF-negative since this LTM 2Q26. The real driver is the CFO collapse rather than rising CapEx — capex has stayed flat at ~$130–140M LTM, while CFO fell from $580M in FY2024 to just $138M in LTM 2Q26, down 76%. They even had to decelerate the repurchase of stock, from −$122M in 2024 to only −$77M over the LTM.

CNR is the odd one out and the only name in the basket generating meaningfully positive FCF. The post-merger start was ugly — Q1 2025 CFO was actually negative (−$110M) on a working-capital drain and integration costs, dragging FY2025 FCF down to a barely-positive +$21M against a −$153M net loss — but the business recovered sharply through 2026. On an LTM 2Q26 basis, CFO of $565M comfortably covers $306M of CapEx for +$260M of FCF, with Q2 2026 alone printing +$149M of FCF and positive net income again. Its met+thermal diversification and much lower CapEx intensity (CapEx ~54% of CFO, vs. above 100% for both HCC and AMR) let it keep repurchasing stock throughout — $240M in 2025 and $149M over the LTM — without turning FCF-negative.

HCC: Scheller appointed CEO and director in March 2016; former CEO of Walter Energy, with a background in mining engineering and roles at Peabody, CNX, and CONSOL. Ten years without turnover. The chairmanship is held by J. Brett Harvey, elected Chairman effective January 1, 2023, after having been a director since 2017 and Lead Independent Director—former chairman of CONSOL, independent. Small board (~7), with mining/finance experience. Only minor nuance: a somewhat aging board.

AMR: With an activist undertone that has already been resolved. Eidson is a career insider: he was President and CFO from 2020 to 2023 before assuming the CEO role in 2023, so the Stetson→Eidson succession was orderly and internal, not a crisis. The chairmanship is now independent: following David Stetson's retirement (effective December 2024, not due to disagreement), Lead Independent Director Michael Gorzynski assumed the role of chairman. An important distinction: Gorzynski is not a "pure" independent director—he is the founder and managing partner of MG Capital Management, a significant shareholder in Alpha, and a former special situations investor at Third Point. He joined the board in 2023 through a negotiated agreement: the company agreed to reimburse an entity controlled by Gorzynski up to $500,000 in legal fees, in connection with an agreement on board composition and the appointment of additional independent directors. In other words, there was activist involvement that was resolved through cooperation and resulted in him becoming chairman—not an escalated dispute, but a chair with a concentrated shareholder agenda.

CNR: It has the weakest governance structure. It was formed from the merger of Arch and CONSOL in January 2025 as a merger of equals, but nine months later Brock (former Chairman/CEO of CONSOL, who was Executive Chairman) assumed the combined role of Chairman and CEO, succeeding Paul Lang, who stepped down as CEO and resigned from the board on October 6, 2025. Lang's departure triggered nearly $8 million in cash severance. There is a counterbalance: Richard A. Navarre (former Chairman of Arch) is the Lead Independent Director. Brock has a strong operational background (over 40 years old, from mine foreman to CEO of CONSOL). The board is very new (average tenure <1 year).
moat_rationale: Here, the main moat is cost, as Warrior is the company in the basket with the lower coal cost, and it's noticing efficient scale thanks to Blue Creek. Even if AMR and CNR are not the best in terms of cost advantages, they have a strong balance sheet, which has allowed them to withstand periods of depreciated coal prices, and they can also achieve efficient scale thanks to projects like Kingston Wildcat (AMR) and the recovery of Leer South for CNR. But the main moat here is the entry barriers in the US, as this kind of company is expensive to establish if you want to invest.

circulo_rationale: The Express & Parcels and Mail operations are easy to understand: physical delivery network monetizing the Iberian e-commerce wave, plus a declining but cash-generative letter business. João Bento led the company from May 2019 and retired at 65; under his tenure with a strong track record. 

Exec committee: now three members — Pacheco (CEO), Joana Freitas (CFO), João Sousa (CCO), the same Sousa credited for playing offense on Cacesa/fulfillment. 

Chairman (non-executive): Raul Catarino Galamba de Oliveira, ex-McKinsey partner (Spain) and independent director at BBVA. 

Board / alignment: shaped by reference shareholders — the Manuel Champalimaud group, Indumenta Pueri, GreenWood Investors and Grupo Sousa, with the de Mello/Champalimaud bloc ~15% the anchor. They issue debt constantly due to their high payout ratio of 30-50%, buyback programs, and the very nature of the business, which requires significant working capital and maturing inventories. Furthermore, Diageo maintains an investment-grade rating and uses inexpensive debt to leverage ROE, a typical behavior for FMCG with stable and predictable cash flows. They also use some debt to hedge against foreign exchange losses, issuing euros instead of dollars.

cashflow_rationale:
Operating cash flow was negative in five of the last six quarters: -$284M, -$434M, +$1,760M, -$159M, -$1,095M, -$289M, for -$501M in total. Only the FY2025 fourth quarter was positive. Against that, $3,313M went out in buybacks and dividends, so $3,814M of shareholder return came from the balance sheet rather than from operations — visible in cash falling from $3,467M at FY2025 year end to $1,184M three quarters later.

Asset-light is marked true post-Millrose: land now sits off balance sheet under option. That is a genuine structural change, though $12,943M of inventory remains and the option fees that replaced ownership are the ACOR drain the thesis says runs until roughly FY27-28.
circulo_rationale: The cycle mechanics are understood: rates drive orders, orders drive volume, volume and incentives drive gross margin. What is less settled is the land-light accounting the company moved to in 2025 — how option fees accumulate as ACOR on the balance sheet and only convert to cost on delivery, and how Financial Services behaves through a downturn when origination volume falls with the homes it finances. The thesis rests on a ~340bps permanent land penalty, which is an estimate of a cost structure that has only existed for one fiscal year.
debt_rationale:
The level is comfortable; the trajectory is not. Net debt/EBITDA is 2.09x on a consolidated basis ($4,818M over $2,302M) and 1.37x on Homebuilding alone ($3,147M), and management's own metric, Net Homebuilding Debt to Total Capital, reads 12.7% at 3Q26 — conservative for a homebuilder.

What earns the yellow is the path. Consolidated net debt went from net cash of $1,506M at FY2023 to $4,818M at 3Q26, and Homebuilding net debt tripled in three quarters, from $643M at FY2025 year end to $2,231M at 2Q26 to $3,147M at 3Q26. FY2025 was the break: the Millrose spin moved $1.0B of cash out and the $1.71B Delayed Draw Term Loan came in.

Consolidated is the basis used here because the model's EPS and EBITDA are consolidated — the "other income" line is Financial Services, so its debt belongs in EV alongside its earnings. The 1.37x adjusted figure strips the Financial Services warehouse, which is secured against mortgage loans held for sale and turns over in 30 to 60 days.
management_rationale:
Capital return is real and the balance sheet is paying for it. The share count fell 7.0% year over year, bought at depressed prices — accretive if the cyclical thesis holds. But over the last six quarters operating cash flow was negative in five, totalling -$501M, against $3,313M of buybacks and dividends: $3,814M of shareholder return funded from the balance sheet, not from operations. Equity shrank 4.5% year over year and FY2026 delivery guidance was cut twice.

GOVERNANCE. Stuart Miller is Executive Chairman and CEO — the roles are combined. Jon Jaffe retired on 31 December 2025 after 42 years and left the board, ending the co-CEO structure and consolidating both seats under Miller. Armando Olivera is Lead Independent Director. Eight non-Miller directors filed Forms 4 in 2026: Hudson, Gilliam, McClure, Sonnenfeld, Olivera, Banse, Wolfe and Smith.

The control structure is dual class. Class B carries ten votes to Class A's one and cannot be transferred outside a defined set of family "Permitted Transferees"; the structure was approved by stockholders in 1987 and again in 2003. Miller holds roughly 19.2% of shares outstanding (~$3.6B), overwhelmingly in Class B, so his voting weight is a large multiple of his economic stake.

That gap drew activism in 2026, and it was governance activism rather than operational. Ahead of the 8 April annual meeting the Illinois State Treasurer asked for vote results broken out by share class, and John Chevedden asked the company to move to one share, one vote. The board recommended against both, arguing the dual class shields long-term decisions from short-term pressure and citing 52% revenue growth over five fiscal years and roughly 300bps a year of outperformance versus the S&P since 1987. Both proposals were voted down.

The conflict worth watching is Millrose. LEN spun off about 80% and retained roughly 20%, and Millrose is externally managed by Kennedy Lewis Land and Residential Advisors under an agreement effective 7 February 2025, with a policy governing how non-Lennar opportunities are allocated between Millrose and Kennedy Lewis affiliates. The practical effect is that the ~340bps of permanent margin penalty in the thesis is a payment stream from LEN to an entity it partly owns, spun off, and does not manage.
moat_rationale:
Scale is real: the #2 builder buys materials, labour and land on terms a regional cannot match, and density within a market lowers the cost of serving it. But the evidence says the moat does not protect price. HB gross margin went from 27.5% in FY22 to 17.7% in FY25 to 16.4% LTM — 1,110bps in three years — while orders fell 9.2% year over year in Q3 FY2026 and the decline accelerated from 3.8% the quarter before. A business that has to buy its buyer with rate buydowns has pricing power only when rates are low.

The land-light model cut into it further. Moving land off the balance sheet traded an ownership barrier for an option fee, and the thesis itself prices that at roughly 340bps of permanent margin. LEN gave up moat for liquidity, deliberately; whether that was the right trade is the whole dispute with the bull case.

cashflow_rationale: Neither of the three. Due to upfront payments Cash From Ops is huge but also CapEx spending so in the last years CapEx is higher, to finance the gap, NBIS is using Debt issuance.
circulo_rationale: Neocloud is a company with servers and data centers for AI computational use by hyperscalers and other companies. Knowledge of energy, semiconductors, and real estate is required. Terms like MW, GW (and ratios related with that), servers depreciation and other energy metrics is required. Also, this is evolutioning constantly.
debt_rationale: $8.1B of ~$8.5B are convertible senior notes. This is not red due to the huge amount of cash that receives from upfront payments to finance the construction of servers and data centers. Also, EBITDA adj. (exc. SBC not like the company) makes the ratio ND/EBITDA still healthy.
moat_rationale: Cost advantage is temporary as efficiency is starting to be reached, and switching costs depend on how they built the software infrastructure, so companies can move data and pipelines to them.

cashflow_rationale:
Operating cash flow was positive in every one of the last 12 quarters, from $1,174M (Q1 FY2024, the Figma fee quarter) to a record $3,160M (Q4 FY2025); LTM OCF is $10,806M and FCF $10,592M, a 40.8% margin and 1.45x GAAP net income. Capex is $214M LTM (0.8% of revenue) and the cash conversion cycle is negative (-27 days) because customers pay up front: deferred revenue is $7.1B. FCF grew at a 10.0% 3Y CAGR from $7.4B in FY2022 to $9.9B in FY2025.

The adjustment that matters is SBC: $2,071M LTM. FCF after SBC is about $8.5B, and that is the figure the P/E valuation implicitly uses, since GAAP EPS carries SBC as a cost.
circulo_rationale: The business model is plain: subscriptions for creative tools (Creative Cloud, Firefly), documents (Acrobat) and enterprise marketing software (Experience Cloud, GenStudio, now Semrush). Subscription revenue was $6,582M of $6,760M in Q3 FY2026 (97%), costs are mostly people, and cash is collected up front. We can read and model it. What is hard to underwrite is the variable that decides the value: whether image and video models, and design tools built on them, replace paid seats or feed them. Management changed the monetization model in Q2 FY2026 (freemium first, Creative Cloud price increases deferred) and changed the reporting in FY2026 (ARR by segment, including Digital Media ARR, dropped in favour of total ARR, and customer-group revenue added; Digital Media and Digital Experience subscription revenue are still reported for Q1–Q3 FY2026), which shortens the comparable history. Green on understanding the business; the AI substitution question is carried in the moat and in the bear case, not here.
debt_rationale:
Leverage is low. At Q3 FY2026 total debt is $6,762M including $399M of leases ($1,597M short-term and $4,766M long-term notes), against $5,639M of cash and short-term investments: net debt $1,123M, 0.11x LTM EBITDA of $10,037M. Excluding leases it is $724M, 0.07x (the adjusted figure). Debt/total capital is 36.5% only because buybacks have shrunk book equity to $11.8B; interest cover is 36x EBIT.

The trend is worth watching, not the level: net debt went from -$3,762M at FY2023 to -$1,830M at FY2024, +$53M at FY2025 and +$1,123M now (3Y average FY2023–FY2025: -$1,846M). The current ratio is 0.77. No convertible notes appear in the FiscalAI debt lines, which are senior notes; this is our reading of the data, to confirm against the 10-K debt note.
management_rationale:
Capital return record is strong and consistent. Shares outstanding fell from 475M at FY2021 to 389M today (-18%), buybacks were $11.3B in FY2025 and $9.3B LTM, funded from FCF of $10.6B LTM. $24.55B remains under the April 2026 authorization. The counterweights: SBC is $2.07B LTM (8.0% of revenue), the 2022 attempt to buy Figma for about $20B ended with a $1B termination fee booked in Q1 FY2024, and the balance sheet moved from $3.76B net cash at FY2023 to $1.12B net debt as buybacks plus the Semrush purchase ($1.56B cash in Q2 FY2026) ran ahead of FCF.

GOVERNANCE. Shantanu Narayen has been CEO since 2007 and is Chair; on 1 December 2026 Anil Chakravarthy (today President, Customer Experience Orchestration) becomes CEO and joins the board, and Narayen becomes Executive Chair, so the chair role stays with a non-independent executive. The team is turning over at the same time: CFO Dan Durn left in Q2 FY2026 (Steve Day is interim CFO), and David Wadhwani, President of Creativity and Productivity, is leaving. Single share class, no controlling holder. Insider ownership is small: Narayen holds 239,123 shares (~$56M, 0.06%) after selling 125,000 shares for about $31.3M on 16–17 September 2026, a week after the succession was announced (FiscalAI insider transactions). Directors hold between ~3,000 and ~35,000 shares each.

Yellow because the capital allocation is good but the next CEO has not yet shown his own framework, there is no permanent CFO, and the incoming CEO comes from the enterprise side while the pressure is on the creative franchise.
moat_rationale:
The moat is visible in the numbers: 89% gross margin, 35% ROIC, revenue up at a 10.5% 3Y CAGR to FY2025 and FCF of $10.6B LTM. Sources are switching costs (workflows, file formats and trained professionals built around Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator and Acrobat), intangible assets (PDF as a standard, the brand, commercially safe Firefly models trained on licensed content) and a network effect in the ecosystem: agencies, freelancers and schools standardize on the same tools.

What earns the yellow is that the moat is not currently converting into pricing. Net new ARR was $400M in Q3 FY2026 against $660M a year earlier (-39%), organic ARR growth is about 9% once the ~$480M of Semrush ARR is removed, RPO has been flat for three quarters ($22.52B, $22.22B, $22.27B, $22.16B), and management deferred planned Creative Cloud price increases to push freemium adoption. Pricing Power is left out of the sources on purpose until price increases stick again. The pressure points: Figma and browser-first design tools in creative, model providers selling generation directly, Salesforce, HubSpot and Oracle in Digital Experience, and DocuSign in documents.
mos_rationale: Price $233.17 (FiscalAI close, 29 September 2026) against a base IVO of $386.78 (15x FY2029 GAAP EPS of $25.79). Green requires price ≤ 0.70 x IVO = $270.75; the stock is 14% below that line, with 66% upside to the IVO (18.4% a year over three years). The bear case at $224.80 sits 3.6% below the current price, so the price already discounts roughly the bear case. 52-week range $193.41 (25 June 2026) to $359.91 (28 October 2025), closing prices.

cashflow_rationale:
CFO was positive in each of the last eight quarters, from $433M (Q2 FY2025) to $897M (Q1 FY2026), and $2,732M in FY2025. Capex is $68M a year, 0.6% of revenue. FCFA2S rose every year from FY2022 ($853M) to FY2025 ($1,683M) and is $2,030M LTM.

Customers prepay maintenance, so deferred revenue ($2,654M at Q2 FY2026) funds working capital, and quarterly cash is seasonal: Q1 is the strongest quarter (FCFA2S $733M in Q1 FY2026) and Q2 the weakest ($345M), partly because of cash-tax timing (CFO, Q2 FY2026 call). FCFA2S converts about 71% of CFO (LTM $2,030M of $2,847M); the difference is interest, lease payments, capex and payments to minorities.

Asset-light: tangible book value is negative (-$5,391M at Q2 FY2026, FiscalAI) because the asset base is acquired intangibles, which is also why reported ROIC (12.1% LTM, FiscalAI) understates the return on the cash actually invested.
circulo_rationale:
The engine is simple to describe: buy small VMS businesses at a hurdle rate, leave them decentralized, recycle the cash. The cash flows are recurring, prepaid and reported in one currency, and the company's own yardstick (FCFA2S) is disclosed quarterly with a reconciliation. That is inside the circle.

What cannot be underwritten from outside is the portfolio itself. About 1,300 businesses in 140 verticals (FY2025) are not disclosed individually, so the AI question (which niches lose pricing power when software becomes cheap to write) cannot be answered bottom-up. On the Q1 FY2026 call management said it cannot classify the portfolio by AI risk in any quantitative way.

Accounting adds noise. Reported net income swings with the IRGA revaluation on Topicus (liability $1,186M at Q2 FY2026) and with amortisation of acquired intangibles, and consolidated figures include Topicus and Lumine at 100% although CSU holds 61.4% of Lumine (Q1 FY2026 MD&A, via press reports) and a minority economic stake in Topicus. On the Q1 FY2026 call the CFO said the company is considering an "economic net income" measure alongside FCFA2S because FCFA2S misses the minority stakes (PEMs) it has started to buy. Green: the model is understood; the opacity of the underlying businesses is carried as a risk, not as a reason to stay out.
debt_rationale:
Leverage is low and mostly ring-fenced. At Q2 FY2026 total debt as FiscalAI counts it is $5,827M: $1,472M with recourse to CSU (US$1B of senior notes at 5.158% due 2029 and 5.461% due 2034, plus the Series 1 debentures, $356M of principal at Q1 FY2026 per press reports of the statements), $2,724M without recourse to CSU (Topicus, Lumine and other subsidiary facilities), $1,186M for the IRGA liability and $445M of leases. Cash is $2,886M.

Net debt of $2,941M against LTM EBITDA of $3,498M is 0.84x. Excluding the IRGA liability, which is the put held by Topicus minorities rather than borrowed money, it is 0.50x (the adjusted figure). Recourse debt alone is 0.42x EBITDA and EBITDA covers interest 11.0x (FiscalAI). 3Y average net debt (FY2023–FY2025, house rule): $2,550M.

Debt to total capital reads 54% ($5,827M over $10,702M), but only because book equity ($4,875M) is small after years of amortising acquired intangibles; it says little about risk here. No convertibles: the senior notes and debentures are straight debt (debenture terms taken from earlier filings, not re-verified for FY2026).
management_rationale:
The capital allocation record is exceptional and measurable: FCFA2S per share went from $40.25 in FY2022 to $79.42 in FY2025 without issuing a share, reinvested at stated hurdle rates. What is not yet proven is the post-founder era.

GOVERNANCE. Mark Leonard resigned as President on 25 September 2025 for health reasons and did not stand for re-election to the board at the 15 May 2026 AGM. Mark Miller, at CSU for more than 30 years and previously head of Volaris, is President; he has waived salary and bonus. Jamal Baksh is CFO and Bernie Anzarouth leads M&A. John Billowits, a former CSU operating executive, has chaired the board since November 2021. Incentives remain distinctive: the bonus plan requires managers to buy CSU shares in the market with part of their bonus, and the CFO confirmed on the Q1 FY2026 call that the plan has not changed. Insider ownership percentages were not verified for this review.

CAPITAL ALLOCATION UNDER MILLER. Deployment accelerated: $1,702M of total consideration in H1 FY2026 against $1,579M in all of FY2025. Deal size rose (DerbySoft ~$400M, TouchBistro, Imagine). Faster deployment is the goal, but it came with higher multiples (the CFO said leverage helped pay more for DerbySoft) and with a 2026 cohort at a 16% margin in Q2 FY2026 against the high 20s to 30s of older cohorts. Yellow until the 2025–2026 cohorts show returns converging to the old ones.
moat_rationale:
At the business-unit level the moat is switching cost in small markets. Mission-critical software embedded in a customer's daily operations, in niches too small to attract a well-funded entrant, is rarely replaced. Management says customers are lost mainly to bankruptcy or consolidation, rarely on price, because retraining users and re-adapting interfaces is painful (Q1 FY2026 call).

The evidence is the recurring line. Maintenance and other recurring organic growth (FX-adjusted) was 6% in FY2022, FY2023 and FY2024 and 5% in FY2025, positive every year, while licences shrank (-18% organic in FY2024, -8% in FY2025). Q2 FY2026 fell to 2% (4% ex-Altera). The CFO attributed the gap to one-offs: prior-year comps at Altera and Dark Matter, a South American customer loss worth about 30bps, and Lumine turnarounds. He expects a return to about 5%.

A second moat sits at head office: reputation as the permanent home for founder-owned VMS businesses, which is why Intangible Assets is included. Competition for deals is still "very robust" (Q2 FY2026 call), so this one protects deal flow, not price. Green with a watch item: two more quarters below 4% ex-Altera would move this to yellow.
mos_rationale: Base IVO is C$4,241 per share (FY2029 FCFA2S of $2,850M at a 4.5% yield, 21.19M shares, 1.419 CAD per USD). 70% of that is C$2,969; the price of C$2,896.47 (TSX close, 29 Sep 2026, FiscalAI) sits 2.4% below it, so the rule gives green, by a thin margin. The 52-week range is C$2,258 (17 Feb 2026) to C$4,030 (3 Oct 2025). The bear case (C$2,225) is 23% below the price; the bull case (C$6,187) is 114% above. The safety is in the multiple: at 21x LTM FCFA2S the stock trades at about half its FY2023–FY2025 year-end average of 40x, so the case needs continued compounding, not a re-rating.

cashflow_rationale: Operating cash flow grew every year from $3,889M in FY2022 to $8,838M in FY2026; capex was $175M, 0.8% of revenue, leaving $8,663M of FCF (FiscalAI). Quarters are seasonal, because the tax season lands in fiscal Q3 (Q3 FY2026 OCF $5,300M against $637M in Q1), but no fiscal year was negative. Two adjustments before calling it clean: SBC was $2,056M, so FCF after SBC is $6,607M and that is the figure to capitalise; and FY2026 OCF was helped by $1,374M of "other adjustments", of which $1,057M came in Q3, so FY2026 FCF growth of 41% overstates the underlying trend (3-year FCF CAGR 21%).
circulo_rationale: The business model is simple to state and each segment's economics can be followed in the filings: subscriptions to accounting and tax software, plus take rates on payments, payroll, small-business loans, and Credit Karma's referral fees on cards, loans and insurance. Green because the mechanics are understood, not because the outcome is. Two parts remain hard to underwrite. First, whether LLM agents take the customer interface away from TurboTax DIY and QuickBooks at the low end. FY2026 evidence is mixed: TurboTax federal units fell from 39.9M to 39.0M and management says price is now the first reason customers leave, while online ecosystem ARPC grew 15% and mid-market revenue 39%. Second, Credit Karma earns fees on partner lending demand, and its revenue fell from $1,805M in FY2022 to $1,634M in FY2023 when lenders pulled back. Both are treated as risks in the valuation, not as gaps in understanding.
debt_rationale: Total debt at 4Q FY2026 was $8,336M including $667M of lease liabilities, against $7,200M of cash and investments, so net debt was $1,136M and 0.17x FY2026 EBITDA of $6,730M (FiscalAI). Excluding leases, net debt is $469M and 0.07x, the adjusted figure. Debt to total capital is 30.5% ($8,336M over $8,336M plus $18,992M of equity). Interest coverage is 23x EBIT. In June 2026 Intuit issued $1.75B of senior notes to pre-fund FY2027 maturities, which is why cash and debt both rose. There are no convertibles. Net debt has fallen from $2,422M at FY2024 and $2,018M at FY2025 (3-year average $1,859M). Customer funds held for payroll and payments sit in current assets and liabilities and are excluded here.
management_rationale:
Operationally sound, and allocation has improved in 2026, but the M&A record is mixed. GAAP operating margin rose from 21.9% in FY2023 to 27.4% in FY2026 and GAAP EPS compounded 25% a year over the same three years. Buybacks rose to $6,121M in FY2026 (cash flow statement), most of it at prices below $450, and SBC is now counted in the non-GAAP figures and guided down to 8% of revenue by FY2030. Against that: Mailchimp, bought for about $12B in 2021 (company press release, not re-verified in FiscalAI), is now flat at about $1.3B of revenue (investor-day figure, unverified) and becomes a separate segment in FY2027, a candidate for impairment or sale. The FY2026 tax season also showed the DIY pricing strategy had been pushed too far.

GOVERNANCE. Sasan Goodarzi has been CEO since January 2019 and became Board Chair as well on 22 January 2026, when Suzanne Nora Johnson stepped down; Vasant Prabhu is Lead Independent Director (company announcement, web). Insiders own little outside the founder: Scott Cook holds 5.64M shares (2.1%), Goodarzi 31K shares directly (FiscalAI insider holders). Insider activity leans to sales: Cook sold about 570K shares at $632-678 in December 2025 and Goodarzi sold 41,000 at $650 in January 2026; the only open-market purchase in the last year was Prabhu's 1,750 shares at about $309 in May 2026. Several securities class actions filed in July-August 2026 allege that the company misrepresented the impact of generative AI on TurboTax, with class periods ending in May-June 2026.
moat_rationale:
QuickBooks is the general ledger of its customers and the file their accountant works in. Moving it means re-mapping years of books, payroll and payment flows, and that is why online ecosystem ARPC could grow 15% in FY2026 while paying customers grew only 3%. More than 150,000 accountants work on the Intuit Accountant Suite and drove 25% of new Intuit Enterprise Suite contracts: that two-sided network is the strongest part of the moat. TurboTax holds tax data on 39.0M federal returns and Credit Karma sees about 1 in 9 US credit card and personal loan originations (company figure).

What earns the yellow is pricing power at the low end. The DIY model raised prices and upsold for years, and in the 2026 season it lost quality DIY filers to low-cost providers. FY2027 guidance cuts DIY prices on purpose and puts TurboTax growth at only 2-3%. The moat protects the complex customer, business or filer; for a simple return or a micro-business, an AI agent plus a cheap filer is now a real substitute.
mos_rationale: Price $268.03 (close 29 September 2026, FiscalAI) against the Base IVO of $478.81: price is 56% of IVO, below the 70% threshold, so GREEN. The Bear case is $234.80, 12% below the current price; the 52-week low was $255.07 on 25 June 2026 and the 52-week high $683.39 in October 2025.

cashflow_rationale:
Operating cash flow has been negative in every fiscal year on record: FY2020 -$20.2M, FY2021 -$53.2M, FY2022 -$43.1M, FY2023 -$17.1M, FY2024 -$25.2M, FY2025 -$27.2M. Over the last six quarters it was -$17.2M, -$6.6M, +$8.4M, -$11.8M, -$16.6M and +$7.2M, for -$36.6M in total. Free cash flow follows the same pattern after ~$3-4M a quarter of capex and capitalised software.

The trend is the argument for patience: adjusted EBITDA went from -$38.4M in FY2023 to $23.0M in FY2025 and $36.0M LTM, and Q2 FY2026 free cash flow was +$6.8M against -$7.4M a year earlier. Management expects conversion to improve in H2 FY2026. Until two consecutive years of positive free cash flow exist, this pillar stays red.

Asset-light is true: capex plus capitalised software ran at 2% of revenue in FY2025 ($8.9M). Stock compensation of $30.6M in FY2025 (6.7% of revenue) is a real cost that adjusted EBITDA excludes.
circulo_rationale:
The product set is understandable: enterprise POS, loyalty, online ordering, back office and c-store software sold on subscription, with terminals and installation at 20-25% margins alongside. ARR is the governing number and it maps closely to subscription revenue (FY2025 subscription revenue $291.2M against $315.4M of year-end ARR).

Two things put it at red rather than green. First, organic growth is hard to read: Punchh (2021), Stuzo and TASK (2024) and Bridg (March 2026) are all inside the ARR series, which compounded 41% a year from FY2022 to FY2025 mostly by acquisition, and from Q2 FY2026 the company stopped splitting ARR and sites between Engagement and Operator Cloud and moved to a single unique-site count. The historic site series therefore does not bridge to the new one. Second, the question the market is pricing is whether AI-native tools erode the value of a restaurant system of record. Management argues the opposite (PAR Intelligence at ~20,000 live sites, 50,000 targeted for FY2026, monetisation in 2027), but there is no revenue yet to test it against. It turns green when two or three quarters of the new unique-site and ARPU series exist and the AI question has a revenue line.
debt_rationale:
All financial debt is convertible notes: $265M of 4.00% notes due March 2031 (convertible at $19.02), $115M of 1.00% notes due January 2030 (convertible at ~$97.00), and the remainder of the 1.50% notes due 2027 after $212M was repurchased in March 2026 (about $53M if the original issue was $265M; hypothesis, not verified against the 10-Q). Total debt including leases is $431.5M against cash of $77.9M, so net debt is $353.6M (FiscalAI, Q2 FY2026); debt to total capital is 0.35.

On GAAP EBITDA (-$12.9M LTM) the ratio is meaningless (-27.3x). On LTM adjusted EBITDA of $36.0M it is 9.8x, and 6.9x on the FY2026 guidance midpoint of $51.5M. That is high, which is why this is not green. It is not red because the structure is benign: low coupons (cash interest roughly $13M a year), no bank debt after the Blue Owl facility was repaid in January 2025, and no maturity of size before 2030 other than the 2027 stub, which cash covers. The cost is dilution rather than default: if the stock rises above $19.02 the 2031 notes add 13.9M shares, 34% of today's count. Net debt history, 3-year average FY2023-FY2025: $298.9M.
management_rationale:
Operating execution improved sharply in 2026: a restructuring in Q1-Q2 cut non-GAAP opex from 48% to 38% of revenue year over year, formal guidance was introduced in May and raised in August (FY2026 adjusted EBITDA $50-53M from $44-47M), and Q2 FY2026 beat the top of both ranges.

The capital allocation record is weaker. Since FY2020 the company has spent about $710M of cash on acquisitions (Punchh, Stuzo, TASK, among others) and raised $546M of equity (FY2020 $132M, FY2021 $216M, FY2024 $198M); goodwill and intangibles of $1,100M exceed shareholders' equity of $814M. The share count went from 27.3M at FY2022 to 41.4M at Q2 FY2026. The March 2026 refinancing replaced 1.5% 2027 notes with 4% 2031 notes convertible at $19.02, and used $33.1M to buy back stock; Bridg was paid with 1.81M new shares ($27.5M) close to the low.

GOVERNANCE. Savneet Singh is CEO and President and a director; James C. Stoffel is independent Chairman (per the 2026 proxy, via press summary). Insiders own little: Singh holds 444,473 shares, 1.07%, and officers sold around $17-18 in March 2026 (Singh 71,915 shares; whether these were tax sales is not verified). Two directors bought in the open market: Keith Pascal 13,000 shares at $15.16 (June 2026) and Narinder Singh 11,518 at $17.36 (August 2026). The largest holder is Voss Capital with 14.3% at 30 June 2026 (13F, FiscalAI), up 21% in the quarter.
moat_rationale:
Switching costs are real at the enterprise end. A POS replacement across thousands of franchised sites takes years: Burger King is rolling out at 400+ sites a month with 3,000+ more planned in 2026, and Papa John's goes live across its US system through the end of 2027. Management says new deals are near-decade contracts and that almost 100% of Q2 FY2026 new engagements were multi-product. Few vendors can serve a Tier-1 QSR at all (NCR Voyix Aloha, Oracle, PAR, and Toast moving up), which is the efficient-scale argument.

What caps it at yellow is pricing power. In Q1 FY2026 PAR had to let a group of Punchh customers go because they paid about 80% below list and would not reprice; organic unique sites fell 2.6% YoY to 145,900 in Q2 FY2026. Loyalty is the more contestable product. Hardware, 26% of Q2 FY2026 revenue, earns ~20% gross margin under tariff pressure and is a pass-through, not a moat. And Toast, with $6.8B of LTM revenue against PAR's $0.5B, is the competitor with the scale to push into PAR's enterprise niche.
mos_rationale: Price $13.51 (29 Sep 2026 close, FiscalAI) against a base-case target of $27.60: the price is 49% of the IVO, below the 0.70x threshold, so green. The 52-week low is $11.82 (close, 10 April 2026). The green is sensitive to the multiple: the bear case gives $8.04, and at 8x rather than 12x FY2029 adjusted EBITDA the base case falls to about $19.10, which is roughly where the 2031 notes convert.

cashflow_rationale:
Free cash flow has been positive in each of the last eight quarters: $97M, $134M, $69M, $208M, $153M, $178M, $115M and $130M (3Q FY2024 to 2Q FY2026, OCF less capex, FiscalAI), for $576M LTM and $608M in FY2025 against $306M in FY2024. Capex is ~$59M LTM, under 3% of recurring gross profit, so the business is asset-light; the only heavy balance-sheet item is hardware inventory, which management chose to build ahead of memory-price increases ($217M at 2Q FY2026 vs $103M a year earlier). That build is why 2Q FY2026 FCF fell to $130M from $208M; management expects conversion to recover in 2H FY2026.

The caveat is SBC: $237M LTM, or 41% of LTM free cash flow. FCF after SBC is ~$339M. The thesis counts SBC as a cost for that reason. Cash flow also benefits from float timing on payment settlement, which can reverse.
circulo_rationale:
The model is simple to follow once revenue is read correctly. Reported revenue ($6,804M LTM) is mostly payments processed gross of card-network interchange, so the 26.7% consolidated gross margin says little. The numbers that matter are the two recurring gross profit streams: subscription ($800M LTM GAAP gross profit, 78% margin in 2Q FY2026) and fintech ($1,282M LTM, ~0.60% of $214.9B of GPV), less the loss on hardware and installation (-$259M LTM). Management guides on exactly these lines, and FiscalAI carries all of them, so the drivers (locations, GPV per location, take rate, ARPU) can be tracked every quarter.

What is less settled: Toast Capital, the lending product, contributed $57M of gross profit in 2Q FY2026 and carries credit risk that is not broken out in a loss table in FiscalAI; and the AI agent products (ToastIQ Grow) and the newer markets (retail, fuel, international) do not yet have disclosed unit economics. Those are small today relative to the core.
debt_rationale:
No financial debt. Cash and equivalents were $1,015M and short-term investments $698M at 2Q FY2026, for net cash of $1,713M (FiscalAI). Net debt/EBITDA is -3.55x on GAAP EBITDA of $482M LTM (FiscalAI) and -2.32x on company adjusted EBITDA of $739M LTM (Q3 FY2025 $176M + Q4 FY2025 $163M + Q1 FY2026 $179M + Q2 FY2026 $221M, company press releases). Operations are well run and the leverage target was met: net debt/EBITDA fell to 2.89x at FY2025 as guided, EBITDA grew 27% in FY2024 and 14% in FY2025, and free cash flow reached €223M (+44%). Against that, 2026 guidance was cut in July (passengers 116–123M → 112–118M, EBITDA €590–650M → €580–630M, capex to below €300M), and the Antalya €7.25bn and Ankara €475M bids were aggressive enough that returns depend on traffic keeping up for 25 years.

GOVERNANCE. Groupe ADP owns 46.12% and runs the company: CEO Serkan Kaptan (since May 2022) also sits on ADP's executive committee in charge of Central Asia, Middle East, Africa, Eastern Europe and CIS, and the board chair, Justine Coutard, comes from ADP. Vice chair Ali Haydar Kurtdarcan. The founders' stake has shrunk to about 4% (Tepe/Bilkent group, unverified). There is no meaningful insider ownership disclosed.

Minority shareholders have little influence. The dividend policy is a 50% payout of net income, which on FY2025's depressed €50.7M produced TL 1.31bn (TL 3.61 per share, about €26M). The risk worth watching is how ADP allocates between TAV and itself — a squeeze-out at a low price, or TAV's balance sheet used for group bids — none of which has happened, but nothing in the structure prevents it.
moat_rationale:
Each airport is a local monopoly for the life of its concession: nobody builds a second terminal in Ankara or Antalya. That is the Intangible Asset (the state licence) and Efficient Scale (one airport per catchment). The dates are long: Ankara 2050, Antalya 2051, Madinah 2041, Almaty owned with no end date. Pricing power is regulated rather than free — aero tariffs are set by the grantor — but commercial revenue is not capped, and duty-free spend per passenger rose 20% to €9.7 in 1H 2026.

The limit is renewal. The moat protects the cash flows during a concession, not the return on the next one: Antalya was won at a €7.25bn auction and Ankara at €475M, so the state captures much of the value at each re-tender. Izmir (end-2032, or 2034 per TAV's site) and Tbilisi (end-2031) are the next ones to face that auction.

moat_rationale:
Two real moats and one eroding. The brands are real intangible assets: Omega, Breguet, Blancpain, Harry Winston, Longines and Tissot cover every price point, and Omega's Olympic timekeeping and the MoonSwatch / Royal Pop collaborations show the portfolio can still create demand (Royal Pop generated more than 25 billion social-media views per the H1 2026 report). The industrial base is the second moat: through ETA and Nivarox-FAR the group makes its own movements, escapements and hairsprings and supplies part of the Swiss industry, a scale position no new entrant can replicate quickly.

What argues against green is share and pricing. Morgan Stanley / LuxeConsult estimate Swatch Group's share of Swiss watch sales at 16.1% in 2025, down 220bps in one year and more than 1,000bps since 2019, with Omega at an estimated CHF 2.2B (-8%) and Longines at CHF 920M (-18%) (third-party estimates; the company does not disclose brand sales). Group gross economics held up (material purchases 17.2% of sales in H1 2026) but the vertical integration turned into a cost when volumes fell: the implied Production loss was about CHF 303M in FY2025. The moat protects existence, not margin.
